name: PT Bank Danamon Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank Danamon: a sub-cost-of-equity franchise with a corporate-action premium
frontmatter.summary: Danamon earns a return on equity below our cost of equity, so fundamental value sits well below book even after crediting the improving margin and asset quality. The share price pays for MUFG's stake decision, not for the franchise. We initiate at SELL with a target of Rp2,995.
thesis: SELL, target Rp2,995, a -33.9% total return including the Rp165 twelve-month dividend. Fundamental value is Rp2,732; the Rp4,780 price is 0.8x FY2026E book against a justified 0.5x.
The spread is structural, not cyclical: sustainable ROE of 8.5% against a 12.5% cost of equity, with the margin fading, a cost base near 56.0% and credit cost held at 2.1% [S10][S4][S3].

Asset quality is genuinely good: gross NPL 1.7%, net NPL 0.1%, loan-at-risk 7.7% and NPL coverage 282.0% [S3][S10]. The base case still carries a through-cycle charge because the auto and SME books are cyclical.
The variant view: the market is capitalising a go-private or sell-down by MUFG, which owns 92.5% of the bank [S15][S16]. We treat that as an event with a real bull case, not as fundamental value.
What would change the rating: a binding buyout at a premium, a durable ROE above the cost of equity, or a cost of equity materially below the sovereign-plus-ERP anchor.

catalysts.event: MUFG reported to be weighing a go-private or a partial sell-down of its Danamon stake
FY2026 results and the FY2026 dividend declaration
Progress on the Danamon-MUFG Indonesia integration and the proposed name change

blocks.text: We initiate Bank Danamon at **SELL** with a twelve-month target of Rp2,995, implying a -33.9% total return from the Rp4,780 price including the Rp165 dividend we expect over the year. Our fundamental value is Rp2,732. The call is not a bet on deteriorating credit: asset quality improved through the year and the margin is at a multi-year high [S10][S3]. It is a bet that a bank earning a return on equity of 8.3% this year and 8.5% at the horizon — a high-single-digit franchise whose ROE never clears the cost of equity — cannot sustain a multiple near book when the rupiah cost of equity is 12.5%.

The market is paying 0.8x FY2026E book for a franchise whose sustainable ROE we put at 8.5% against a 12.5% cost of equity. On a justified P/BV of 0.5x that book is worth Rp2,973. The residual-income model comes in below at Rp2,582 and the dividend-discount model lower again at Rp2,354 because the payout is only 35.0% [S0]. The weighted value is Rp2,732, and the target adds a year of book-value growth and the dividend.

The honest counter-case is corporate action. MUFG owns 92.5% and the public float is 7.5%, far below the OJK minimum public shareholding rule [S15]. MUFG has been reported to be weighing a go-private transaction or a sell-down to lift the float [S16], and the integration with MUFG Indonesia is under way with a proposed name of PT Bank MUFG Danamon Tbk [S8]. A buyout at a premium would invalidate a SELL. But the report is explicitly at the rumour stage: the discussions are internal, no decision has been taken, MUFG declined to comment, Danamon has not responded, and no buyer, price or binding proposal is in print [S16][S15]. We therefore disclose the event, size the price at which it would bite and leave it out of the base case rather than pay for a number nobody has published — see the valuation section.

Three things move the value. First, credit cost: each percentage point of cost of risk is worth a sizeable share of parent profit, and the auto and SME books are the cyclical exposure [S10]. Second, the margin: the nine-month margin of 8.0% is at the top of the range, and deposit competition can take it back toward the FY2025 level of 7.7% [S10][S4]. Third, the discount rate: at a cost of equity anchored on the long sovereign yield plus the house equity-risk-premium band, the justified multiple stays below book unless sustainable ROE rises well above our estimate [S17][S18].

Bank Danamon is a mid-sized Indonesian commercial bank and the Indonesian platform of Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group. It reports four commercial engines: Enterprise Banking and Financial Institutions, SME Banking, Consumer Banking, and the subsidiaries led by Adira Finance in auto and multipurpose financing and Home Credit Indonesia in consumer credit [S10]. The group employed 23,722 people at the last count and is headquartered in Jakarta [S0]. Its history runs back to the founding generation of Indonesian private banking and it has operated under the Danamon name for half a century [S0].

Danamon began as a small trade bank, was recapitalised through the Asian financial crisis, and spent the two decades after it building a retail and auto-finance franchise. Adira Finance gave it a national auto-lending distribution network; MUFG's control turned it into a Japanese group's main commercial-banking vehicle in Indonesia. Its competitive position is that of a well-capitalised challenger with a specialist consumer book rather than a nationwide deposit franchise.

At the end of FY2025 the group carried IDR212,700.0bn of total credit and trade finance, up nine per cent like-for-like, and IDR176,900.0bn of third-party deposits, up sixteen per cent [S5]. The mix matters: enterprise and financial institutions grew fastest, consumer banking next, SME more slowly and Adira only marginally in FY2025 [S5]. By September 2026 the mix had rotated further toward corporate: enterprise and financial institutions were up a fifth year on year, SME and the subsidiaries grew high single digits and consumer banking mid single digits, taking total credit and trade finance to IDR232,600.0bn [S10]. That is a faster-growing, lower-yield book than the auto loan book, which is why the margin fade in our forecast is structural rather than cyclical.

Deposits reached IDR190,500.0bn at September 2026, up twelve per cent [S10]. The franchise is built on granular funding: current and savings accounts were IDR75,200.0bn at end-FY2025, up eighteen per cent, or a little over two-fifths of the deposit base [S4]. That CASA ratio is respectable for a bank of this size but well below the large state and private incumbents, and it is the main reason the cost of funds is sensitive to competition. The consolidated loan-to-deposit ratio is 120.2%, above the system norm because Adira's receivables are consolidated while its funding is partly raised outside the bank deposit base [S0][S5]. The group therefore runs a structurally tighter liquidity position than a plain commercial bank, which we treat as a funding risk rather than a modelling error.

The strategy is explicit: one financial group built around the Tumbuh Bersama promise, leveraging MUFG's global network for cross-border corporate and trade business, Adira's auto ecosystem for consumer credit, and Home Credit for mass-market consumer finance [S10]. The integration with MUFG Indonesia is in progress and the proposed name is PT Bank MUFG Danamon Tbk [S8]. Group structure is simple: MUFG Bank, Ltd is the controlling shareholder with 92.5%, and there is no listed intermediate holding company above Danamon [S15][S0]. The practical consequence is that minority shareholders own a small sliver of a bank whose strategy, capital and dividend are set by a single foreign parent.

On market position, Danamon is a challenger, not a leader. System credit is roughly forty times Danamon's own book [S17], so this is a low-single-digit market share. It competes on distribution and product breadth in auto and SME lending rather than on deposit cost or scale. That is a defensible niche, but it is not a moat: the auto-finance advantage is a distribution relationship that other multifinance arms also have, and the corporate push depends on MUFG's balance sheet rather than on Danamon's own pricing power [S10].

The Indonesian banking system is growing faster than the economy. Credit rose 13.3% year on year to September 2026, led by investment and corporate credit, while working-capital and consumer credit grew more slowly [S17]. Deposits grew 8.2%, well below credit, so the system loan-to-deposit ratio is rising and deposit competition is the binding constraint on margins [S17]. Asset quality is stable: system gross NPL 2.1% against a much lower net ratio and a loan-at-risk figure around four times the gross NPL [S17]. Danamon's own gross NPL of 1.7% and loan-at-risk of 7.7% are better than the system, which is a genuine positive and one reason we do not model a credit blow-out [S3][S10].

Policy is the second driver. Bank Indonesia held its policy rate at 5.8% at the October meeting, citing rupiah stability [S18]. Our macro deck carries the policy rate at 5.8% for FY2027E, real GDP growth of 5.3% and consumer inflation of 3.3% for the same year, with the rupiah at 18,350. A stable-to-lower policy rate helps deposit repricing, but the balance-of-payments pressure in our macro regime means the rupiah, not the policy rate, is the swing variable for foreign-owned banks. Danamon's earnings are entirely rupiah-denominated, so translation risk is nil, but a weaker rupiah raises imported cost pressure and can force the central bank to keep real rates high, which caps the margin recovery.

The sector deck's driver for banks is the policy-rate path, and our macro regime is cautious on Indonesian rate-sensitive names. We have not imported that view as a blanket haircut: the base case uses the company's actual nine-month margin and a gradual fade, not a collapse. But it does mean we do not give Danamon credit for a large margin expansion from falling rates. The FY2025 margin of 7.7% and the nine-month figure of 8.0% already capture most of the benefit of the higher-rate environment [S4][S10].

Competitive positioning is best judged against the listed peer set. Bank Central Asia owns the deposit franchise and earns a return on equity far above its cost of equity; Bank Rakyat Indonesia and Bank Mandiri have scale and state-linked funding; Bank Negara Indonesia has a similar corporate book at a much larger size; the regional banks compete for the same SME and consumer customers. Danamon's differentiators are MUFG's cross-border network, the Adira auto ecosystem and Home Credit's consumer distribution [S10]. Its disadvantages are a small deposit base, a CASA ratio below the leaders, and a cost-to-income ratio near 57.7% that reflects sub-scale [S0]. Five-forces view: rivalry is high and rising; the threat of new entrants is low for a licensed bank but high in consumer lending from fintech; supplier power is deposit competition; buyer power is rising with rate transparency; and substitutes are the capital markets and digital wallets. The net position is a narrow, non-durable advantage, which supports a valuation below book rather than a premium.

Indonesian banking is a spread business regulated by the financial services authority and the central bank, with a deposit-insurance backstop, minimum capital and liquidity ratios, and a long history of consolidation. Foreign ownership of a listed bank is permitted within limits, and several Japanese, Malaysian and Singaporean groups control mid-sized Indonesian banks. Sector returns are set by the funding mix and credit cost rather than by product innovation, which is why a gap in CASA share is so persistent.

Two regulatory developments matter for the multiple. The minimum public shareholding rule puts Danamon and CIMB Niaga, two foreign-controlled banks, in a compliance window [S15]. MUFG's options are to sell down, which increases the float and could improve index inclusion, or to go private, which removes the listing entirely [S16]. Separately, the exchange's treatment of concentrated-ownership names has become a market-wide issue in 2026 [S15]. For Danamon the practical effect is that the free float, not the fundamentals, determines marginal supply. A sell-down to the floor would put a block equal to a large multiple of one day's traded value into an illiquid register, so it would clear only at a concession and over an extended period — a supply overhang, not a fundamental change; a go-private removes the minority's liquidity at a price the parent chooses, and the same article notes that a controller buying back at a depressed valuation is the pattern that costs minorities most [S15].

The earnings base is a high-margin, high-credit-cost consumer and SME bank. FY2025 net interest income was IDR18,215.2bn on the data pack's definition and non-interest income IDR4,472.8bn, together IDR22,688.0bn of operating income [S0]. On the company's narrower definition operating income was IDR21,600.0bn and non-interest income IDR3,700.0bn, the difference being how subsidiary and sharia income are classified [S5]. We use the data pack for the history and the company's reported ratios for the margin and cost commentary, and we flag the definitional gap rather than smoothing it away. The company's margin was 7.7% in FY2025, up from 7.3% in FY2024, and reached 8.0% in the first nine months of 2026 [S4][S12][S10]. An alternative nine-month calculation published alongside the results puts the consolidated margin at 7.6%, reflecting a different treatment of subsidiary income [S3]. We use the company's headline figure because it is the basis on which guidance and the FY2025 comparison are given, but the gap is a reminder that a few tenths of a percentage point of margin is worth several per cent of earnings. On the basis the model actually uses, the FY2025 figures reconcile: net interest income of IDR18,215.2bn over earning assets of IDR236,607.5bn reproduces the reported 7.7% [S0][S4], while the lower alternative calculation puts 9M2026 at 7.6%, up about thirty basis points year on year [S3] — the same move the company series shows from the FY2025 level to the nine-month figure [S4][S10]. The two are parallel series about forty basis points apart at the same observation date, not a restatement of one another.

The 9M2026 comparatives are not on the FY2025 data-pack base, and the difference is a disclosure, not a red flag. The company restated prior-period comparatives under PSAK 338 for two common-control business combinations: the Mandala Multifinance and Adira merger, effective 1 October 2025, and the additional Home Credit Indonesia stake bought from Adira, effective 24 June 2026. The company states these are accounting presentation adjustments that treat the transactions as if they had occurred from the start of the common control period, made to improve comparability [S10]. Two consequences follow. First, the thirteen per cent loan growth and nineteen per cent profit growth quoted for 9M2026 are measured against restated comparatives, not against the data pack's FY2025 lines, so we do not read them as organic growth on our own base. Second, the HCI transaction raises the group's share of HCI profit from its effective date, which is why we hold the minority take at the FY2025 actual rather than letting it drift down. The data pack's FY2025 history is the audited, pre-restatement base; we use it for the history and the restated growth rates only for the direction of travel [S0][S10].

Costs are the weak point. FY2025 operating expenses, derived as the pack's operating income less the reported pre-provision profit of IDR9,600.0bn, were IDR13,088.0bn, a cost-to-income ratio of 57.7% [S0][S4]. On the company's narrower operating income the ratio is nearer 56.0%, and the nine-month run-rate is about the same [S10]. We hold the ratio flat at 56.0% through the forecast. That is a deliberate change from our first draft, which assumed the MUFG integration would take three points out of the ratio: the only archived disclosure describes a legal-entity merger and a proposed name, not a cost programme with targets [S8], so the improvement had no source. The corporate build-out adds relationship and compliance cost before it adds fee income, and the integration could as easily add cost as remove it. If the company publishes a synergy target, the ratio is the first line we would revisit.

Provisions are the swing factor. FY2025 loan-loss provisions, derived as pre-provision profit less the pack's pretax profit, were IDR4,214.0bn, about two per cent of average loans [S0][S4]. The nine-month 2026 charge was IDR3,810.0bn, down five and a half per cent year on year, which annualises slightly above the FY2025 full-year ratio because the fourth quarter of FY2025 carried a low charge [S3]. Asset quality indicators are strong: gross NPL 1.7%, net NPL 0.1%, loan-at-risk 7.7% and NPL coverage 282.0% [S3][S10]. The FY2025 loan-at-risk ratio was 8.3% and coverage improved through 2026 [S4][S10]. The releases do not break out special-mention or restructured balances, which is a gap in the evidence: the loan-at-risk ratio is the only published measure that captures the restructured book, because the company's definition includes the extended COVID-era restructurings [S12], and it is the series we lean on. Our base case holds credit cost at 2.1% for the whole forecast — above the FY2025 outturn of 2.1% and in line with the nine-month annualised run-rate — and does not fade it back toward a trough quarter. That is a through-cycle charge for an auto and SME book, and it is the single most important reason our ROE stays below the cost of equity.

Capital and funding are comfortable but not free. The FY2025 capital adequacy ratio was 25.4%, and our estimated risk-weighted-asset density of 1.00 times loans implies a capital ratio of 23.9% in FY2026E, drifting to 20.8% by FY2035E as loans outgrow retained earnings [S4]. That is far above the regulatory minimum, so growth is not capital-constrained; the constraint is deposit funding and the parent's capital allocation. The consolidated loan-to-deposit ratio is 121.3% in our FY2026E forecast and rises modestly as loans outgrow deposits [S0][S10]. We hold deposit growth close to loan growth for that reason. A funding shock, not a capital shortfall, is the realistic liquidity risk.

Profitability is the crux. FY2025 ROE was 7.4% on our model, rising to 8.3% in FY2026E and holding around 8.5% to the end of the forecast on loan growth and a flat cost ratio [S0]. That is a high-single-digit franchise, not a distressed one: the nine-month run-rate supports the first step, with parent profit of IDR3,500.0bn annualising on the same equity base [S10], and no year in the forecast falls to a mid-single-digit return. Our FY2026E parent profit of IDR4,610.4bn is consistent with a fourth quarter slightly below the nine-month average, reflecting seasonal provisioning and integration cost. The long-run ROE never reaches the cost of equity, which is the mathematical core of the SELL.

Capital allocation is straightforward. The FY2025 dividend was Rp142 per share, a payout of 35.0% [S0]. The five-year dividend record runs from Rp118 in FY2022 to Rp142 in FY2025, with a dip in FY2024 [S0]. We hold the payout at 35.0%: MUFG takes most of the cash, but the bank retains enough to fund high-single-digit loan growth without new equity. There is no rights issue, buyback or special dividend announced [S10][S15].

Earnings-quality flags, per the house screen. For a bank the accrual ratio is not meaningful, so we use provisioning and asset-quality trends instead: provisions exceed the NPL-implied charge, coverage is 282.0%, and loan-at-risk is falling, which is the opposite of borrowing earnings from the future [S10][S3]. Divergence flags: loan growth is in line with system credit growth of 13.3%, not outrunning it; there is no receivables or inventory cycle to check; margin expansion is matched by improving asset quality rather than by deteriorating cash conversion [S17][S10]. IDX regime flags: the stock is not on the special monitoring board and carries no special notation in the sources reviewed, but its free float of 7.5% is below the minimum, which is a structural overhang rather than a manipulation flag [S15]. Related-party gravity: MUFG is the controller and the integration is the main related-party channel; the releases do not quantify related-party lending or fee flows, and we have not assumed any [S8][S10]. Structure flags: no pledged controller shares are disclosed in the archived releases; the controlling stake is held by a regulated bank, not a family vehicle [S15]. Provisioning trend: the nine-month charge fell year on year while coverage rose to 282.0% and loan-at-risk improved, which is a conservative rather than an aggressive pattern [S3][S10]. Classification: no manipulation-class flag found. The definitional margin gap, the PSAK 338 restatement of the 9M2026 comparatives for the two common-control transactions, the FY2024 comparative restatement and the low free float are optics-class flags that we disclose and account for [S3][S10][S15].

We value Danamon on residual income, justified price-to-book and a dividend-discount cross-check, which is the house method for banks and the right one here. A bank's value is its book equity plus the present value of the spread between return on equity and cost of equity; a discounted-cash-flow model on free cash flow is meaningless because deposits and loans are the operating assets. The weights are 50.0% justified price-to-book, 30.0% residual income and 20.0% dividend discount, matching the sector configuration.

The cost of equity is pinned, not selected. The long rupiah sovereign yield is 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2% and the Indonesia country risk premium 2.5%. With a beta of 0.90 and the sector's 1.6% default spread, the mechanical result is about 12.5% after our 0.6% premium. The premium is not a risk fudge: the house bank card pins cost of equity at the sovereign yield plus a mid-single-digit Indonesian equity risk premium, and our figure sits at the low end of that band once the engine's beta and default-spread treatment are applied. We deliberately use the low end, because Danamon's capital ratio of 25.4% and its MUFG backing are credit positives. A higher cost of equity would lower the value further.

The primary method is justified price-to-book. Sustainable ROE is 8.5%, and it is the model's terminal-year ROE rather than an early-years average: a warranted multiple discounts a perpetuity, so the ROE that belongs in it is the one the franchise settles at, not the one it starts from. The path is built from the forecast: the margin runs from 8.0% to 7.6%, the cost-to-income ratio is held at 56.0%, and credit cost is held at 2.1%. With terminal growth of 4.0%, the justified multiple is the difference between sustainable ROE and terminal growth over the difference between cost of equity and terminal growth, or 0.5x.

The book value base matters here and we state it plainly. The engine applies the multiple to the latest reported parent book value in the data pack — the current book, not next year's — and that is the base that reproduces the method value of Rp2,973. Applying 0.5x to our FY2026E book value per share of Rp5,882 would give a higher number; we do not do that because next year's retained book is added in the roll-forward to the target, not twice. The model's book value per share grows from Rp5,553 to Rp7,406 over the forecast [S0].

Two things are deliberately outside the methods. The first is the corporate action. A go-private at book value per share of Rp5,882, or at the premium the market would expect, is worth more than our bull case and more than the current price; a partial sell-down lifts the float and removes the supply overhang but leaves the franchise economics unchanged, which is why it should not move fundamental value. Neither is in the base case because the only sourcing is a report that the options are being weighed internally, with no decision, no buyer and no price [S16], and the parallel analysis of the free-float issue describes the Danamon plan as still rumour [S15]. We size the level at which the event bites and let the reader apply a probability; the rating is wrong in the world where a binding offer at book appears, and we say so.

The second is the capital surplus. Our estimated capital ratio is 23.9% in FY2026E, falling to 20.8% by FY2035E on the 35.0% payout and our loan growth, so the buffer is being consumed by growth rather than sitting idle [S4][S0]. There are also two sourced reasons not to capitalise it today: the integration with MUFG Indonesia creates a larger Indonesian legal entity that will absorb capital [S8], and no buyback or special dividend is announced [S10]. Economically, a distribution would be worth more than the book multiple we apply, so a capital-return announcement is an upside risk to this call — but it is not something the company has said it will do, and paying for it in the base case would be an invented assumption.

The residual-income model gives Rp2,582, -13.1% versus the primary method. It is the same economics in a different form: opening book value of IDR54,269.5bn plus the present value of residual income in every forecast year, which is negative because ROE never clears the cost of equity. The terminal value is negative too. It lands below the warranted multiple because the residual-income path charges the gap year by year while ROE climbs from 8.3% to 8.5%, whereas the warranted multiple applies the settled ROE immediately. The dividend-discount model gives Rp2,354, -20.8% versus the primary method, because a payout of 35.0% on a low ROE produces a thin dividend stream relative to the discount rate. Both cross-checks land below the primary method and inside the divergence threshold, which is the expected ordering for a bank whose ROE stays under the cost of equity: the dividend model ignores the value of retained book and the residual-income model charges the gap year by year.

How to read the divergence: the dividend model would only match the primary method if the payout rose toward the level of a mature utility, which MUFG has not signalled and which the growth plan does not support [S10]. The residual-income model sits below the warranted multiple because it discounts the actual path, where the spread is negative in every year, rather than assuming the settled ROE applies from today. We weight the primary method most heavily because it is the cleanest statement of the franchise economics and the least sensitive to the terminal-value mechanics.

The sensitivity table shows the two variables that matter. A half-point change in sustainable ROE moves the justified multiple by roughly a tenth of book, and a one-point change in the cost of equity moves it by more. At a cost of equity a point lower and sustainable ROE half a point higher, the justified multiple would be around a quarter of book above our number; at a cost of equity a point higher and sustainable ROE half a point lower it would be roughly a tenth below. The current price of Rp4,780 is 0.8x FY2026E book, which is consistent with a sustainable ROE well into double digits at our cost of equity, or with a cost of equity close to the sovereign yield. Neither is our base case. A reverse discounted-cash-flow is not meaningful for a bank; the price-to-book-implied ROE is the right reverse test, and it says the market is capitalising a franchise materially better than the one the accounts show.

The target of Rp2,995 is the weighted value rolled forward twelve months plus the Rp165 dividend. The -37.3% figure is the price move to our target before the dividend; the -33.9% total return, which adds the Rp165 dividend, is the rating input. No liquidity discount is applied: the stock's three-month average daily traded value is IDR16.2bn, above the floor at which the house applies an explicit haircut to the target [S0]. That is a statement about trading, not about the float: with a public holding of 7.5% the daily value turns over a large share of the free float every few weeks, so the same number that clears the liquidity floor is the number that makes a placement of the controller's stake a long, discounted process [S15].
The downside risks, ranked by likelihood times impact:

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Why it matters | |---|---|---|---| | Credit cost normalises above our through-cycle charge | Medium | High | Auto and SME books are cyclical; a one-point increase in cost of risk takes a large bite out of parent profit [S10][S3] | | Deposit competition compresses the margin | Medium | High | CASA is only a little over two-fifths of deposits; system deposit growth lags credit growth [S4][S17] | | MUFG goes private at a price that ignores minorities | Low | High | A controlling holder with 92.5% can set terms; the float is 7.5% [S15][S16] | | Rupiah and balance-of-payments pressure force the central bank to stay tight | Medium | Medium | Higher real rates cap margin recovery and raise credit stress [S18][S17] | | Regulatory change to free-float or index rules | Medium | Medium | The public shareholding rule and exchange treatment of concentrated ownership are live issues [S15] | | Governance and related-party concentration | Low | Medium | MUFG sets strategy, capital and dividend; minority influence is minimal [S15][S8] | | Liquidity and funding | Low | Medium | The loan-to-deposit ratio is 121.3%; a deposit outflow would force asset repricing [S0][S5] |

Credit cost is the first risk because the improvement is real but the base is a consumer book. The nine-month charge of IDR3,810.0bn annualises above the FY2025 ratio, and the auto segment is sensitive to used-car prices and employment [S3][S10]. A move from our 2.1% to a materially higher cost of risk would take FY2026E parent profit down by a sixth or more and push the justified multiple toward the bear case. The second risk is the margin: the nine-month peak of 8.0% is the high-water mark, and the FY2025 level of 7.7% is the more normal base [S10][S4]. If deposit costs reprice faster than loan yields, the margin gives back the 2026 gain.

Governance risk is unusual here: the main risk is not expropriation but the parent's option. MUFG has been reported to be considering a go-private transaction or a sell-down [S16]. A go-private at a premium would be good for minorities who are bought out; a go-private at a low price, or a long period of uncertainty, is bad for anyone who needs liquidity. The public shareholding rule gives MUFG a reason to act, but not a timetable we can source [S15].

The bear case at Rp2,225 assumes credit cost rises, the margin gives back part of its gain and loan growth slows; the bull case at Rp3,943 mirrors those shocks with the same magnitudes in the opposite direction. The base case at Rp2,907 carries a 50.0% probability, with the bear and bull at 25.0% each. Weights are set on relative likelihood, not on outcome size, and the outcomes are not symmetric even though the shocks are: the bear loses Rp2,225 of value per share from the base and the bull adds Rp3,943. That is not an artefact. A warranted price-to-book multiple is linear in ROE, so when ROE falls toward terminal growth the numerator of the multiple shrinks toward zero and the value is floored by book and the residual-income path, while a bull case that lifts ROE also lifts the multiple applied to a growing book. The convexity is the correct economics of a bank that destroys value in the bad state.

The bull case is not a takeout: it is the fundamental path in which credit cost falls and the margin holds near its peak, and it still sits below the current price because even then ROE does not clear the cost of equity. What is missing from all three scenarios is the corporate action and the capital surplus. A binding offer at or above book value per share of Rp5,882 would break the SELL, and a decision to distribute the surplus built up under a 23.9% capital ratio would be worth more than the book multiple we apply. We carry both as event risks with a disclosed level and no probability, because the sources describe internal deliberation and publish no price [S16][S15], and we would rather be visibly wrong in that world than invent the number that avoids it.

Signposts that would change the view: a binding buyout proposal with a price; a sustained decline in cost of risk back below its FY2025 level; a CASA ratio above half of deposits; a cost-to-income ratio below the peer median; and a cost of equity below the sovereign-plus-ERP anchor on a lower sovereign yield. On the downside: loan-at-risk rising back above its FY2025 level, NPL coverage falling sharply, a deposit run that pushes the loan-to-deposit ratio well above its current level, or a regulatory sanction on the free float.

Ownership is the defining governance fact. MUFG Bank, Ltd controls 92.5% of the shares; the public holds 7.5%, below the regulatory minimum [S15]. The free float is the lowest in the peer group alongside CIMB Niaga, and the exchange's concentrated-ownership regime has made low-float stocks a market-wide issue in 2026 [S15]. MUFG has been reported to be weighing a go-private transaction or a partial sell-down to lift the float [S16]. The proposed integration with MUFG Indonesia and the name change to PT Bank MUFG Danamon Tbk are the visible corporate actions [S8].

Board and management are MUFG-aligned. The president director is Nobuya Kawasaki and the finance director is Muljono Tjandra, both with long tenure in the group [S0]. The board's independence is limited by the parent's voting control; minority shareholders have no practical ability to block a related-party transaction that the parent supports. That is not a finding of misconduct, but it is a reason to require a wider margin of safety in the valuation, which our cost-of-equity premium partly reflects.

Related-party dealings: MUFG is the controlling shareholder and the integration is the main channel; the archived releases do not quantify related-party lending, fee-sharing or funding arrangements, and we have not assumed any [S8][S10]. Pledged shares: nothing in the archived releases indicates that the controlling stake is pledged [S15]. Auditor and opinion: the sources we could archive do not include the auditor's report, so we do not opine on it; the FY2025 figures are from the company's results release and the data pack [S4][S0]. Dividend record: the dividend per share path from Rp118 in FY2022 to Rp142 in FY2025 is progressive but not a commitment; the payout is 35.0% and the parent is the main recipient [S0].

ESG exposures are typical for an Indonesian consumer bank: financial inclusion is a positive, auto lending carries a transition-risk exposure through the used-vehicle collateral pool, and data privacy and responsible-lending conduct are the main social risks. Governance is the dominant ESG factor here because of the controlling stake. We do not apply a separate ESG discount; the low free float and the parent's control are already reflected in the cost-of-equity premium and in the event risk in section five. On the positive side, the bank's capital ratio of 25.4% and its NPL coverage of 282.0% are conservative balance-sheet settings that reduce tail risk [S4][S10].

The near-term catalyst is the FY2026 results and dividend, expected in February 2027 [S10]. We will compare the FY2026 outturn with our IDR4,610.4bn parent profit and Rp165 dividend per share, and we will re-underwrite the credit-cost path if the fourth-quarter charge is materially above the nine-month run-rate [S10][S3]. The MUFG stake decision is the event that could break the SELL: a binding offer at a premium, or a sell-down that lifts the float, would change the supply and the index treatment [S16][S15]. The integration with MUFG Indonesia and the proposed name change are the medium-term catalysts [S8].

The KPIs we monitor between updates: quarterly loan and deposit growth against the system; CASA ratio and cost of funds; the margin against its nine-month peak; cost-to-income against our 56.0%; gross NPL, net NPL, loan-at-risk and NPL coverage; provisions and the annualised cost of risk; capital adequacy and risk-weighted-asset density; and any disclosure on related-party flows, pledged shares or the free float. We also track the long sovereign yield and the rupiah, because they drive the cost of equity and the credit cycle more than any company-specific variable [S17][S18].

The main non-financial swing factor for a bank like Danamon is the credit cycle in used vehicles and small business. Used-car prices, employment in the informal sector, and the pace of motorcycle and car sales determine both demand for Adira's product and the recovery value of collateral. None of these is disclosed at a granular enough level to model separately, so we capture them in the credit-cost scenario rather than in a separate volume line.

S0.title: Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile for BDMN.JK

S15.title: Foreign banks, delisting and the 15% free-float test (Feedberry)

S16.title: MUFG weighs future of Danamon stake (Tribun)

bear.narrative: The auto and SME book cracks as the rupiah pressure of the BoP regime slows domestic demand: credit cost rises 60bp, the margin gives back 40bp as deposit competition intensifies and BI is forced to tighten, and loan growth stalls three points. NPL coverage of 282% cushions the P&L but the return on equity falls further below cost of equity.

bull.narrative: Asset quality keeps improving and the MUFG integration delivers: credit cost falls 60bp, the margin gains 40bp from cheaper MUFG funding and CASA growth, and loan growth runs three points faster as the corporate pipeline converts. A go-private or sell-down at a premium becomes more likely, but the base case does not pay for it.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs NIM and credit cost
12-month value vs cost of equity and terminal growth

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 total credit and trade finance of Rp232.6tn is up 13% yoy, led by enterprise and financial institutions (+20%), SME (+9%), consumer (+5%) and the subsidiaries (+7%) [S10]; system credit grew 13.26% over the same period [S17]. We hold 13% for FY2026 (the fourth quarter is seasonally the strongest for the corporate book), then fade to 8% by FY2030 as the MUFG-driven cross-border pipeline matures, still above the 6% terminal rate that nominal GDP supports.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: Consolidated deposits of Rp190.5tn at September 2026 are up 12% yoy [S10], well ahead of system deposit growth of 8.22% [S17] because Danamon is winning current and savings accounts. The consolidated loan-to-deposit ratio is already above 120% (Adira funds itself partly outside the bank deposit base), so deposit growth must track loan growth to avoid funding pressure: 12% in FY2026, then 10%, 9%, 8.5% and 8%, with a 6% terminal rate.

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: Derived from the reported margin, not assumed: FY2025 net interest income of Rp18.2tn at a 7.7% NIM implies average earning assets of about Rp236.6tn against average loans of roughly Rp204tn, i.e. 1.16x [S0][S4]. At September 2026 loans are Rp232.6tn inside Rp301.3tn of assets (June balance sheet, the latest available), so the earning-asset ratio is near 1.12x [S10]. We use 1.14x flat; the securities and placement book grows with the deposit base.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the company series that reconciles to our net interest income history: FY2025 NII of Rp18.2tn over earning assets of Rp236.6tn is 7.70%, exactly the 7.7% the company reports [S0][S4], and 9M2026 is 8.0% on the same series [S10]. The 7.57% calculation published alongside the results [S3] is a parallel series, not a restatement: it shows 9M2026 at 7.57% against 7.26% a year earlier, the same roughly 30bp move the company series shows from 7.7% FY2025 to 8.0% 9M2026 [S4][S10], but about 40bp below it at the same date; dropped into this model it would understate interest income by a twentieth. We therefore use 8.0% and fade 10bp a year to 7.6% as the lower-yield corporate book grows, with BI held at 5.75% [S18]; the 7.57% calculation stays a disclosed cross-check.

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: FY2025 non-interest income of Rp3.7tn grew 9% yoy, with treasury income up 64% [S5]. We do not extrapolate the treasury spike: fee income grows 8% a year on the MUFG and Home Credit distribution agreements, easing to 6% and then 6% terminal as the bancassurance and wealth cross-sell matures. 9M2026 operating income grew 5% with NII doing the work, so 8% NOII growth is not a stretch.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: Held flat, because no archived source discloses a cost programme. FY2025 operating expenses are about Rp13.1tn on the data pack's Rp22.7tn operating income against Rp9.6tn of PPOP, a 57.7% ratio [S0][S4]; on the company's narrower Rp21.6tn operating income the ratio is nearer 55.6% [S5]. For 9M2026, PPOP of roughly Rp8.3tn on Rp19.0tn of operating income implies about 56% [S10]. The MUFG Indonesia integration is disclosed as a legal-entity merger and name change, not as a cost programme with targets [S8], so we start at 56% and hold it: the corporate build-out adds relationship and compliance cost before it adds fee income.

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: Held at the reported run-rate, not faded: FY2025 provisions are about Rp4.2tn (PPOP Rp9.6tn less PBT) or roughly 207bp of average loans [S0][S4], and 9M2026 provisioning of Rp3.81tn annualises to about 228bp [S3]. We hold 2.1% flat — between the audited year and the nine-month run-rate — for the whole forecast, and do not assume the charge falls back toward the trough quarter. Asset quality is genuinely better (gross NPL 1.71%, net NPL 0.08%, loan at risk 7.7%, NPL coverage 282% [S3][S10]) but LAR includes the restructured book [S12], so the improving trend is an input to the risk case, not to a lower through-cycle charge.

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: engine default constant; no recurring non-operating line is disclosed

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Held at the FY2025 actual: minorities took Rp223.5bn of Rp4,194.2bn consolidated profit, 5.3% [S0]. The 9.82% additional HCI stake bought from Adira (effective 24 June 2026) lifts the group's share of HCI [S10], but minority balance-sheet interests rose to Rp7.1tn and we do not assume a lower profit share until the reported ratio shows it.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 DPS of Rp142.19 against EPS of Rp406.27 is a 35% payout; FY2024 was 32% (Rp113.85/Rp356.35) [S0]. MUFG owns more than 92.47% [S15] and takes the dividend as its return, but the bank also needs to fund 8-13% loan growth and keeps 65% of earnings. We hold 35% through the forecast; no state-ownership payout rule applies.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: engine default constant; no rights issue or buyback is announced and the free-float fix is a sell-down by MUFG, not new shares

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: Derived from the disclosed capital ratio: FY2025 KPMM of 25.4% [S4] on consolidated equity including minorities of about Rp58.0tn implies risk-weighted assets near Rp228tn against Rp212.7tn of loans, i.e. about 1.07x [S0][S5]. We use 1.0x, slightly conservative to the bank's own ratio, because the Adira receivables and the corporate book both carry close to full credit risk weight.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: 4.0% nominal sits below the 5.0% IDR terminal cap and below the BI policy rate of 5.75% [S18]: it is the long-run inflation path plus modest real growth, not an extrapolation of the current 13.26% system credit growth [S17]. Deposit and loan growth both converge to this rate.

challenges.challenge: Base and bull assign zero probability to the live MUFG corporate action (S16) even though the summary says a premium buyout 'would invalidate a SELL'; bull Rp5,386 is only +12.7% and built from mirrored fundamentals, below a plausible 1.0-1.2x book takeout (Rp5,550-6,660).
challenges.answer: The corporate action is now sized and disclosed in the summary and in the valuation section: a takeout at the FY2026E book value per share, or at a premium, sits above both our bull case and the current price, and we say the rating is wrong in that world. It stays out of the base and the probability weights because the only archived sourcing is a report that the options are being weighed internally, with no decision, no buyer and no price, and the parallel CIMB case is described as rumour [S16][S15]. We do not invent a probability or a buyout multiple that no source states; the level at which the event bites is published for the reader to weight.

challenges.challenge: Excess capital is never valued: CAR 25.4% and model CAR 21.8-22.3% through FY2035E versus a regulatory floor implies roughly Rp12-17tn (Rp1,200-1,750/share) of distributable surplus, yet payout is fixed at 35% and no buyback or special dividend is modelled.
challenges.answer: The surplus is now addressed on the model's own numbers rather than asserted away: the estimated capital ratio falls from 23.9% in FY2026E to 20.8% by FY2035E on the 35% payout, so the buffer is being consumed by growth, and two sources explain retention — the MUFG Indonesia integration creates a larger Indonesian legal entity that will absorb capital [S8] and no buyback or special dividend is announced [S10]. We state plainly that a distribution would be worth more than the book multiple we apply, so it is an upside risk to the SELL rather than a base-case input.

challenges.challenge: The 15% free-float rule requires MUFG to shed ~7.3pp of its 92.5% stake (about Rp3.4tn at Rp4,780) into a float trading ~Rp16bn/day (200+ days of ADTV), but the bear case shocks only credit/NIM/growth and section 2 calls a sell-down 'dilutive to the price only in the short run'.
challenges.answer: Section 2 no longer calls a sell-down dilutive only in the short run. It now says a block equal to a large multiple of one day's traded value would clear only at a concession over an extended period, and that a controller buying back at a depressed valuation is the pattern that costs minorities most [S15]. The ADTV paragraph makes the same point: the same 16.2bn a day that clears the liquidity floor is what makes the placement long and discounted [S0][S15].

challenges.challenge: The earnings-quality screen reads NPL, net NPL, LAR and coverage levels but never restructured or special-mention loans or the PSAK 71 provisioning trend, and S10 note 2 shows the 9M2026 comparatives were restated under PSAK 338 for the Adira/Mandala merger and the 9.82% HCI acquisition, so the 13% loan and 19% profit growth are not on the FY2025 data-pack base.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now reconciles the bases: the 9M2026 comparatives are restated under PSAK 338 for the Mandala/Adira merger (1 Oct 2025) and the additional HCI stake (24 Jun 2026), which the company describes as presentation adjustments for common-control combinations [S10], so the 13% loan and 19% profit growth are against restated comparatives and the HCI closing-date effect is why we hold the minority share at the FY2025 actual. Special-mention and restructured balances are not broken out in any archived release; we say so and use loan-at-risk, whose definition includes the extended COVID-era restructurings [S12], plus the coverage and provisioning trend [S3][S10].

challenges.challenge: The justified P/BV uses roe_sustainable 8.63% (the average of FY2026-28) as a perpetuity ROE while the model's own ROE rises to 9.83% (FY2030E) and 9.68% (FY2035E); at 9.68% the justified multiple is 0.672x, worth ~Rp3,735 vs Rp3,042.
challenges.answer: The warranted P/BV now uses the model's terminal-year ROE (FY2035E 8.52%) via an explicit valuation.roe_sustainable override instead of the engine's average of FY2026-28: a perpetuity multiple takes the ROE the franchise settles at, not an early-years average. The path is flat after FY2028 at 8.4-8.5%, so the correction is small on the rebuilt base but it is the right number, and section 4 says so [S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the 0.547x multiple is 'Applied to FY2026E book value per share of Rp5,866, that is Rp3,042', but the engine applies it to BVPS Rp5,557.8 (market equity Rp54,319.5bn / 9,773.6m shares); 0.5474 x 5,866 = Rp3,211, so the stated arithmetic does not reproduce the number.
challenges.answer: The mislabelled book value is corrected. Section 4 now states that the engine applies the justified multiple to the latest reported parent book value in the data pack, not to FY2026E book, and that this is the base that reproduces the method value; applying 0.53x to the FY2026E book value per share of Rp5,882 would give a higher number and we explain that next year's retained book is added once, in the roll-forward to the target, not twice [S0].

challenges.challenge: ADTV is written 'IDR16,216,323.10tn', twelve orders of magnitude above the model's 16,216,323,103 (Rp16.2bn), so the 'well above the fund's threshold' no-liquidity-discount conclusion is unreproducible and rests on a threshold the report never states.
challenges.answer: ADTV is restated in the correct unit: the placeholder now formats the 16,216,323,103 rupiah figure as IDR16.2bn a day, not trillions, and the paragraph states that this is above the floor at which the house applies an explicit liquidity haircut, which is why no discount is taken. It also notes that the same number is small relative to the block a float fix would require [S0][S15].

challenges.challenge: The summary and section 3 call the ROE 'mid-single-digit' while the model shows 7.4% (FY2025A), 8.0% (FY2026E), 9.8% (FY2030E), and 9M2026 Rp3.5tn annualises to ~8.6% on Rp54.3tn of equity; the prose understates the franchise and overstates the gap to a 0.8x multiple.
challenges.answer: The 'mid-single-digit' description is gone. The summary and section 3 now describe the ROE as modelled — 8.25% in FY2026E and around 8.5% to FY2035E, a high-single-digit franchise — using placeholders, and the SELL is rebuilt on that path: the ROE never reaches the 12.45% cost of equity, which is the valuation case rather than a claim of distress [S0].

challenges.challenge: The only BLOCK flag (drift.cti) is justified by S8 ('shared technology and compliance functions') and S10 (9M CTI near 56% on Rp19.0tn), but S8 reports only an integration process and a proposed name change, and S10 gives neither PPOP, opex nor CTI, so the 3pp cost-income improvement has no source that says so.
challenges.answer: The 3pp cost-income improvement is withdrawn rather than justified with a source that does not say it. CTI is now held flat at 56% through the forecast: the only archived disclosure of the MUFG integration describes a legal-entity merger and a proposed name, not a cost programme with targets [S8], and 9M2026 only supports the starting level [S10]. The drift.cti BLOCK clears because there is no drift, and section 3 says what we would need to see to restore an efficiency path.

challenges.challenge: The BI policy rate is given as '5.8%' twice, including 'our macro deck carries the policy rate at 5.8 rate for FY2027E', against 5.75% in S18 and the deck; terminal_growth is also sourced to S17 for the macro deck's 5.29% real GDP and inflation anchor, and S17 contains neither.
challenges.answer: The policy rate is no longer typed: section 2 uses the macro deck placeholder, which resolves to the reviewed 5.75% [S18]. The terminal-growth basis previously credited S17 with the macro deck's real GDP and inflation path, which S17 does not contain; it now cites the BI rate of 5.75% [S18] and uses S17 only for the 13.26% system credit growth it does report.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E NIM is set at 8.0% on the company headline basis while S3 publishes a 9M2026 consolidated NIM of 7.57% (up from 7.26%); using 8.0% rather than 7.57% overstates NII by about 5%, and the model then fades to 7.5%.
challenges.answer: We checked the arithmetic and the 7.57% calculation is a parallel series, not the comparable consolidated margin. FY2025 net interest income of Rp18.2tn over earning assets of Rp236.6tn is 7.70%, exactly the 7.7% the company reports [S0][S4]; the 7.57% calculation shows 9M2025 at 7.26% where the company series showed 7.3% for FY2024 [S12], so it sits about 40bp below the company basis throughout and both series move by the same ~30bp into 9M2026 [S10][S3]. Dropping 7.57% into a model fed by the company's consolidated NII would understate interest income by a twentieth, so we keep 8.0% and section 3 discloses the reconciliation and the cross-check.

challenges.challenge: Credit cost ends at 1.9% (190bp), below the FY2025 actual ~207bp and the 9M2026 annualised ~228bp, and minority_pct is held at 5.1% vs the FY2025 actual 5.3% while minority balance interests jumped to Rp7.1tn - both flatter parent profit.
challenges.answer: Credit cost is no longer faded below the actual: it is held at 2.1% for every forecast year, between the FY2025 outturn of 2.10% and the 9M2026 annualised run-rate of about 2.28% [S0][S3][S4]. Minority share is set to the FY2025 actual 5.3% and the basis explains that the additional HCI stake raises the group's share from mid-2026 while the Rp7.1tn minority balance argues against assuming a lower take [S0][S10].

challenges.challenge: Bear and bull shock the same drivers by mirrored amounts (credit +/-60bp, NIM -/+40bp, growth -/+3pp), yet the outcomes are Rp1,649 (-65%) vs Rp5,386 (+13%); the asymmetry comes from the P/B numerator (ROE-g) approaching zero, and the probability-weighted target depends on it with no sourced reason.
challenges.answer: The five-fold asymmetry was mostly an artefact of the unsourced optimism in the old base: with CTI held flat and credit cost held at 2.1%, the bear is Rp2,225 and the bull Rp3,943 around a Rp2,907 base, a ratio of about one-and-a-half times, with the same mirrored shocks. What remains is explained in section 5: a warranted P/BV multiple is linear in ROE but its numerator approaches zero as ROE tends to terminal growth, while the bull lifts ROE and the book it is applied to. We keep the weights at 25/50/25 because they reflect relative likelihood, and we do not double the bear weight to force symmetry.

challenges.challenge: Facts F33-F36 (earning assets, opex, provisions) are computed numbers attached to quotes that state only PPOP or loans (S4), so the load-bearing ~207bp FY2025 cost of risk is an estimate presented as a sourced fact.
challenges.answer: F33-F36 are now explicitly labelled 'Computed, not disclosed' with a derivation field naming the components and the scale that bridges the quoted figure to the value: loans times the 1.1124 earning-asset bridge for the two earning-asset facts, and PPOP minus the data-pack operating income or PBT for opex and provisions [S5][S12][S4]. The ~210bp FY2025 cost of risk is now quoted in section 3 from the model's own derived credit-cost line, not presented as a disclosed fact.

missing_bull_case.note: The live MUFG go-private / sell-down (S16) is excluded from base AND bull even though the summary says a premium buyout would invalidate a SELL; bull Rp5,386 is only +12.7% and is built from mirrored fundamentals, below a plausible 1.0-1.2x book takeout. Excess capital (CAR 25.4%, model CAR 21.8-22.3%) of roughly Rp12-17tn is never valued or tested as a capital return; the MUFG cost/NOII synergy the base CTI path assumes is also absent from the bull shocks.

missing_bear_case.note: The 15% free-float rule forces MUFG to shed ~7.3pp of its 92.5% stake (~Rp3.4tn) into a float whose ADTV is ~Rp16bn/day (~200+ days of volume), but the bear case shocks only credit/NIM/growth and the report calls a sell-down dilutive only in the short run. Restructured/special-mention loans and the PSAK 71 provisioning trend are not examined, and S10 note 2 shows the 9M comparatives were PSAK 338 restated, so the 13%/19% growth is not clean against the FY2025 data-pack base.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E NIM of 8.0% is taken on the company headline basis while S3 publishes a 9M2026 consolidated NIM of 7.57% (from 7.26%); the higher basis adds ~5% to NII. Terminal credit cost of 1.9% is below the FY2025 actual ~207bp and the 9M annualised ~228bp, and minority_pct is held at 5.1% vs the FY2025 actual 5.3% while minority balance interests jumped to Rp7.1tn. Loan growth fades 13% to 8% and NIM fades to 7.5% on narrative, not sourced data.

evidence_and_citations.note: Section 4 states the 0.55x multiple is applied to FY2026E BVPS Rp5,866 but the engine uses Rp5,557.8, so the stated arithmetic gives Rp3,211 not Rp3,042. ADTV is written IDR16,216,323.10tn against an actual Rp16.2bn (twelve-order unit error). The drift.cti justification cites S8 for shared technology/compliance and S10 for a 9M CTI, but neither source states a cost plan. Terminal growth cites S17 for the macro deck's 5.29% GDP/inflation, which S17 does not contain; S15 is a secondary web source for the load-bearing 15% rule; F33-F36 derived numbers are attached to quotes that give only PPOP/loans.

valuation_method_fit.note: Residual income, warranted P/BV and DDM are the right bank methods, weights 50/30/20 match the card, COE 12.45% is at the low end of the sovereign+5.0-6.0% band and the components reproduce, and the negative RI terminal value is handled consistently. The flaw is the primary method: roe_sustainable is the FY2026-28 average (8.63%), applied in perpetuity to BVPS Rp5,557.8, while the model's own terminal ROE is 9.68% and the label says FY2026E BVPS.

bias_and_tone.note: The summary and section 3 call the ROE mid-single-digit while the model shows 7.4% (FY2025A), 8.0% (FY2026E) and 9.8% (FY2030E), and 9M2026 Rp3.5tn annualises to ~8.6% on Rp54.3tn equity; the prose understates the franchise and overstates the gap to 0.8x book. Bear and bull are described as mirrored but deliver -65% vs +13%, and the conclusion leans on an 8.6% number the model itself does not hold as terminal.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Bank COE 12.45%, g 4%, IDR basis and credit cost are consistent with the published BANKS comps, and BDMN at 0.815x FY2026E P/B is the most expensive low-ROE name versus BBNI 0.684x BUY, BJBR 0.431x ADD, BJTM 0.519x BUY - so the SELL direction matches the deck. But the BI rate is stated as 5.8% twice (including the FY2027E deck path) against 5.75% in S18 and the deck, and the macro GDP/inflation figures are mis-sourced to S17.

conservatism_audit.note: Below-terminal/unsourced conservatism: sustainable ROE 8.63% vs model terminal 9.68% (worth ~Rp690/share on justified P/B, ~Rp390 on the target); corporate action and Rp12-17tn excess capital at zero value; MUFG synergy omitted from the bull. Offsetting optimism: NIM 8.0% on the higher published basis, terminal credit cost 1.9% below the last actual, minority 5.1% below 5.3%, ea_loans 1.1124 while its own basis text says 1.14x. The conservatism stack (with C1/C2) is enough to halve the -25% return and must be resolved by the Sector Lead.

calibration.note: The calibration gate shows FY2026E ROE 7.98% versus FY2025A actual 7.38% (+60bp), which the report never explains; it is supported by the 9M2026 run-rate but should be reconciled explicitly. The single BLOCK flag (drift.cti) is marked justified on a source (S8) that reports only an integration process and a proposed name change, so the justification does not meet the gate's own standard.

signoff.notes: SELL rests on a name-specific, sourced driver: sustainable ROE 8.5% vs COE 12.45% at 0.8x FY2026E book, justified P/B 0.5x; not the house long-bank call restated. Both counter-cases that could break it (MUFG go-private or sell-down S16; Rp12-17tn capital surplus) are disclosed, sized and excluded with sourced reasoning, so the SELL is the residual after paying for neither, not dressed-up caution. Remaining FIX do not move TP 2,995: Q1 must read bear -Rp682 (-23.5%) and bull +Rp1,036 (+35.6%) vs the Rp2,907 base, not the bear/bull values; Q2 average-vs-year-end EA NIM convention; Q3 rwa_density 1.0 is generous not conservative vs implied 1.07 and is car_est only. Correct in rendering.

bias.note: Base FY2026E ROE 8.25% vs FY2025A 7.38% is sourced (NIM 8.0% on 9M2026 [S10], loans +13% [S10]); CTI held 56% against a company-basis 55.6% FY2025 [S4][S5] (no drift; pack basis prints 57.7%); credit cost 2.1% flat is mildly above the audited 2.10% but below the 2.28% 9M annualised (slightly optimistic); NIM fades to 7.5% terminal, 65bp on the model series (slightly conservative). Scenarios shock the same three drivers by mirrored amounts (credit +/-60bp, NIM -/+40bp, growth -/+3pp) with base 50%. SELL survives the favourable corner: at COE 11.85% with no premium and ROE 8.6% the justified P/B is 0.586x, about Rp3,255, still roughly -30%.

recomputed.item: FY2025A NIM on model average-earning-asset basis (pct)

findings.finding: Section 5 states the bear 'loses Rp2,225 of value per share from the base' and the bull 'adds Rp3,943'. Those are the bear and bull VALUES (engine 2,225 / 3,943 around base 2,907); the deltas are -Rp682 and +Rp1,036. As written the sentence says the bear loses 77% and the bull adds 136%, which is not what the engine does and contradicts the paragraph's own asymmetry argument.

The NIM basis says the FY2025 history reconciles to the reported 7.7% (NII Rp18,215.2bn / earning assets Rp236,607bn), but ea_loans 1.1124 was calibrated on YEAR-END earning assets while the engine computes nim_line on AVERAGE earning assets: the model prints FY2025A NIM 8.145%, 44bp above the reported 7.7% [S4]. Applying the 8.0% input to average EA gives FY2026E NII Rp20,159bn; on the year-end basis the report's own arithmetic implies Rp21,389bn (+6%). The 7.7%-vs-7.57% rebuttal to C11 rests on the year-end basis, so it does not reconcile the model series it defends.

rwa_density 1.0 is described in the basis as 'slightly conservative to the bank's own ratio', but the bank's own FY2025 KPMM of 25.4% on about Rp58.0tn of equity implies RWA density near 1.07x [S4][S0]. At 1.07 the FY2026E car_est is about 22.3%, not 23.9%, and FY2035E about 19.4%, not 20.8%. Using 1.0 overstates the capital buffer and therefore the surplus the C2 answer relies on. The target is unaffected (car_est is not a valuation input).

The NIM input fades 8.0% to 7.5% terminal (65bp on the model series, 20bp below the FY2025A company-reported 7.7%), while the last three observations rose 7.3% to 7.7% to 8.0% [S12][S4][S10]. The only support is the corporate mix shift; no source fixes the magnitude. At 20bp on roughly Rp500tn of earning assets this is worth high single digits per cent of value.

F6 quotes S10 as 'dan deposito sebesar Rp190,5 triliun', but S10 reads 'total rekening giro, rekening tabungan (CASA) dan deposito sebesar Rp190,5 triliun'. The value is total third-party funds, not time deposits; the truncated quote mis-describes the line it supports.
Section 5's risk table gives the loan-to-deposit ratio as 121.3% without a period, next to 120.2% in section 1; they are FY2026E and FY2025A respectively. Readers will read it as a contradiction.

Section 4 says a 50bp higher sustainable ROE and a 1pp lower COE puts the multiple 'around a quarter of book above our number'. The arithmetic gives 0.669x vs 0.535x, i.e. +0.13x of book (+25% relative), not a quarter of book.

The judge files the BI rate as '5.8%' against F32/S18 5.75%. Both instances are placeholders (fact.F32 and deck.macro.bi_rate.FY2027E) rendered at one decimal, not typed numbers; no stale figure is present.
